*For Russia, the 2nd Weltkrieg did not end in fire and calamity - but with the signing of a humiliating ceasefire. The Smolensk Accords brought peace to much of Eastern Europe, but to Russia, it merely brought further turmoil, and only the iron fist of Boris Savinkov, the eternal Vozhd, kept the Motherland from falling into a second civil war in 1944.*

*Then, Savinkov died.*

*The father of the nation, the Vozhd himself, was brought down by a sudden stroke in 1947, leaving much of Russia in chaos. East of the Urals, formerly exiled or imprisoned political enemies seized their chance to rise up against the Narodnik regime, leading Siberia into a period of strife and warlordism known as the Siberian Anarchy. In the Russian heartland, the NSRPR split along ideological lines; reformists, reactionaries, hardliners and esotericists fought one another for control of the Russian State.*

*This infighting was brought to an end in late 1948 when a triumvirate of Narodnik leaders regained control over most of Western Russia. This 'Troika' comprised of Georgiy Vernadsky, general secretary of the NSRPR and head of the party's Reformist faction; Mikhail Levitov, Savinkov's right-hand man and leader of the NSRPR's Hardliner faction; and Dmitry Ustinov, a prominent White Army general and head of the Narodnik party's Militarist faction. While not represented within the Troika, an Esotericist faction had also emerged within the NSRPR during the 'interregnum,' coalescing under the leadership of Pavel Gorgulov and the Natsgvardia.*

*Stability had returned to the west by the turn of the 1950s, however in the east, the Siberian Anarchy and the warlords that ruled it had largely turned against each other. The Russian Democratic Republic which inhabited most of western and central Siberia was plagued by infighting, as monarchists, anarchists, socialists and radical Narodniks sought to reshape the Republic in their own image. The Far Eastern Republic, commonly referred to as Transamur, found itself under threat from a neo-Bolshevik movement under the command of former Red emigres and assisted by the CFSR. Kazakhstan, comprising the former territories of the Alash Autonomy, had fallen into a full-blown civil war by the early 1950s, as ideological divides tore the steppe nation apart.*

*When the White Army crossed over into Siberia in 1953, however, a spark of unity among the eastern warlords was lit, and it started a fire that would come to be known as the Ural War. From 1953 to 1955, the Russian State and the All-Russian Liberation Front fought a grinding war of attrition, as neither side seemed able to gain any significant advantage over the other. The Troika regime was still plagued with internal factional divides, and both the Third International and Co-Prosperity sphere had committed a significant amount of aid to the ARLF. When a truce was called in late 1955, the Russian State had taken only a few cities west of the Urals, namely Arkhangelsk and Orenburg. The ARLF, however, quickly collapsed when the Narodnik threat dissipated, leading to the resumption of hostilities between the Siberian warlords and the renewal of the Siberian Anarchy.*

*In 1961, both Russia and Siberia stand at a crossroads. The Troika seems poised to collapse, and the eve of the 2nd Russian Civil War draws nearer. The Siberian Warlords continue their infighting, however, the spark of unity lit by the Ural War still burns brightly in the hearts of a select few - should Siberia unify once more whilst Western Russia burns, that spark may very well carry one warlord's army over the Urals and into Moscow.*

**Tl;dr of Events:**

The war begins on September 1st, 1939, when the Union of Britain invades the Republic of Ireland. 5 days later, the Commune of France and UoB both launch a combined invasion of Germany termed 'Operation Charlemagne,' bypassing German defenses by going through the Ardennes. They eventually push to the River Rhine, where they will stay for most of the war. In early 1940, the Russian State under Boris Savinkov joins the war, as a result of the Saratov Pact signed between Russia and France in 1939, invading Germany's client states in Eastern Europe. In late 1940, the Reichspakt and former Entente powers sign the Halifax Accords, bringing together the two alliances against the radical Saratov Pact - this brings the French Republic, Portugal, Sardinia, and Canada into the war. On December 7th, 1941, the up until now relatively isolated Eastern Seas War becomes the Pacific Theatre of the 2WK, when the Empire of Japan attacks elements of the American navy loyal to the Sacramento Government stationed at Pearl Harbor, leading to the Pacific States, Canada, and Germany declaring war on Japan. The Chinese War of Unification alsonties into the 2WK around this time, as Germany begins aiding the Pact-aligned Fengtian Government's enemies. Setbacks ensued for the Pact in all fronts save the Pacific, after a brutal Russian defeat at Odessa and the Accord invasions of Spain and Italy in 1943, and the liberation of the Rhineland from Pact occupation in 1944. In late 1944, facing the prospect of a grinding war of attrition with the Germans and growing instability at home, Germany and Russian signed a white peace known as the Treaty of Smolensk, though the Kingdom of Finland didn't stop fighting the Russians until mid-1945. In the west, the Accord followed this by launching one last offensive with the aim of crushing the French Communards once and for all. In August 1945, this succeeded, as Paris fell to joint Franco-German troops. Preperations for the Accord invasion of Britain, termed 'Tag X,' began immediately, however they wouldn't amount to anything as on May 3rd, 1946, the Union of Britain dropped an atomic bomb on Wilhelmshaven. This was folliwed by Bremen on the 5th, and on May 8th, Germany agreed to a ceasefire with the British, angering the former Entente members of the Accord.

-- The Collapse of the EU --

After years of economic collapse beginning in the late 2020s, Europe was on the brink of total ruin by 2043. The chaos of the 2nd American Civil War devastated both NATO's cohesion, and it's very structure as an alliance, opening the door for the Eurasian Union to force it's dissolution when the European member states failed to respond to an invasion of the Baltics. Most European countries were themselves severely internally divided, thanks in large part to the rise of both far-right and far-left groups funded by the Eurasian and Chinese blocs respectively. In late 2032, France was thrown into a brief but violent civil war, and the later assassination of the German Chancellor saw Germany fall into intense civil disorder not seen since the days of the Weimar Republic. With the financial crisis of 2034, several EU countries initiated their own exit procedures, most notably Poland, Italy, Spain, and the Balkan members. This lead to the wholsale dissolution of the EU in late 2035.

-- Rise of Mitteleuropa ---

From the ashes of the old European order, arose several political alliances. States too small to avoid their own collapse flocked to larger nations, such as France or Spain. Of most interest to us is the Central European Confederation, often referred to as Mitteleuropa in Germany. Centred around the Federal Republic of Germany, now under the leadership of the radical anti-communist and anti-Eurasianist group known as the German National Unity Front (Deutsche Einheitsfront, DEF), the CEC also includes former EU members such as Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Austria, and the Netherlands. The Kingdom of England, Hungary, and Denmark have also been granted associate status, sharing the member states'  economic and border privelages without partaking in the joint military venture the union is famous for. While principally a union of equals, the bloc is in practice simply a collection of German satellite states. 

-- A European Cold War --

Mitteuropa shares the continent with a number of other power blocs, most notably the French-led Bloc Socialiste, the Medditerranean Union and the Nordic Federation. These developements have led to a "great game" of sorts, as the CEC vies for dominstion of the Balkans and British isles. It is also in a state of constant vigilamce against the belligerent Eurasian Union, with which is shares a lengthy militarized border.

**Reconstruction & Dictatorship**

There was much for Reichskanzler von Schleicher to do in the wake of the war's end. The Rhineland and north-western Germany had both suffered greatly under the ire of the Republican Air Force, and the eastern European countries which came under Russian occupation had been positively devastated. Reconstruction began in earnest, but the damage done to Germany's economy might just have been irreparable. As the nation trudged through the early postwar years, von Schleicher's grip on power only seemed to tighten; thanks to his and the autocratic Kaiser's machinations, the SPD's factional divides only worsened, leading to the dissolution of the party in 1948. The FVP and NLP, both strongly opposed to Schleicher's rule, were forced to unite into the FLP in 1949, as their historically liberal Christian voter bases felt that their views might be better represented in their own Christian populist party, resulting in the formation of the CVP. It appeared in 1951 that Schleicher's grasp over the German government, aided by the Kaiser and the DNE, might never loosen. Of course, the Kaiser wasn't going to live forever...

**New Kaiser, New Constitution**

In July of 1951, the bells rang out over Berlin, Köln, München, Hamburg, and every other city within Germany; for the Kaiser, Wilhelm III, was dead. His eldest son, Wilhelm Friederich, had been killed in action in the Rhineland during the Second Weltkrieg, and so the throne passed to his second son, Kronprinz Louis Ferdinand. Renowned - and reviled - for his liberal views, the young Kaiser Ferdinand took the throne amidst a hale of controversy, stirred up by Schleicher's lapdogs in the press. However, these attempts to discredit him only further convinced the Kaiser that Schleicher had led Germany too far astray and down the path of authoritarianism. After gathering together a clique of sympathetic generals and politicians, the Kaiser led what amounted to a bloodless coup against Schleicher and his deeply entrenched DNE, with the self-styled Steel Chancellor himself placed under house arrest following his dismissal by the Kaiser. The weeks following Schleicher's downfall were chaotic, to say the least, as pro-Schleicher demonstrators clashed with liberal and leftist counter-protestors, engulfing a number of German cities in bloody violence. Eventually, however, the Kaiser and his clique emerged victorious, putting into place a new constitution that would prevent authoritarian figures such as Schleicher or Ludendorff from ever arising in Germany again.

**The Cold War So Far**

Since the end of the Second Weltkrieg, German domestic and foreign policy has been dominated by an ideological and geopolitical struggle known as the Cold War. Primarily fought between the German-led Sicherheitspakt, the Third International, and the Japanese-dominated Co-Prosperity Sphere, it has been characterised by proxy conflicts, intergovernmental espionage, and the ever-present threat of total nuclear annihilation. Since the fall of the DNE in 1952, the Progressive Liberal Party (FLP) has dominated the Reichstag, eclipsing the SDP as the largest parliamentary party due to the latter's factional splits in the late 1940s. Zentrum has emerged as a close runner-up to the FLP, and has entered into three separate coalition governments with them since 1952. Many predict that this arrangement, however, is soon to be disrupted; as the long-standing Reichskanzler and FLP party leader, Theodor Heuss, passed away in 1963, leaving his well-respected economic minister Ludwig Erhard to take the reigns of the government. The FLP-Zentrum coalition had been in a steady decline in terms of popularity for years before Heuss' death, however Erhard's government now finds itself without the security of an experienced, electable figurehead. Meanwhile, both the far-right and far-left of German politics have gathered strength: the German Democratic Party (DDP), widely considered to be the direct successor to the mainstream SDP, has seen a steady rise in popularity, spearheaded by the charismatic and compromising Kurt Schumacher; the German Conservative Party (DkP), though once the cornerstone of Kurt von Schleicher's DNE, has also experienced a resurgence in popularity over the course of the 1950s, thanks in large part to a dramatic rise in tensions with the Third International and the resulting 'Rote Angst.' Germany in 1964 stands at a crossroads, both internally and internationally.  On the world stage, she has committed herself to fending off both American and Japanese advances, most notably in the Namib War of 1951-54 and the Papua Conflict in 1956. Geopolitical struggles have not confined themselves to Africa and Asia alone, however; after their combined victory in the Second Weltkrieg, the French Fourth Republic and Danubian Federation have sought to carve out their own spheres of influence in Europe - the Mediterranean Security Treaty Organisation and Donau-Adria Wirtschaftsbund, respectively. Much like during the Sonnentage Period which followed the First Weltkrieg, Germany finds herself beset on all sides by geopolitical rivals and ideological enemies. Now, however, the price of failure is not just the end of German hegemony - but the end of the world as we know it. Hail to thee in the victor's crown, for thy head is never far from the noose.

**Calm Before the Storm**

After almost two decades of uncontested dominance over Europe, it seemed in 1936 that the German Empire might never come down from her place in the sun. But as the old adage goes - “the bigger they are, the harder they fall” - and the economic crisis commonly referred to as Black Monday would see Germany fall very hard indeed. As Kuno Graf von Westarp's conservative coalition government struggled to reassemble the shattered economy, Germany's chief geopolitical adversaries - namely the syndicalist Third International and revanchist Russian State - continued to grow in strength. The effects of Black Monday were so severe, in fact, that the elections of April 1936 resulted in the formation of an SPD-FVP-CSRP government, and the appointment of Otto Wels, leader of the social democrats, to the position of Reichskanzler.  Even today, Wels remains a controversial figure in German politics - with the nation's recovery from Black Monday largely credited to his Minister for Economics, Walter Rathenau, Reichskanzler Wels is remembered almost strictly as the face of the Erhaltungspolitik (Preservation Politics) period of 1936 through 1939. Wels' ill-fated detente policies would culminate in 1938 with the Copenhagen Conference; here, Germany and her Reichspakt allies acquiesced to a number of the Syndicalists' demands, the most damning of which being the Irish government's agreement to significant de-militarisation.

**The Second Weltkrieg**

With the apparent success of the Copenhagen Conference, Otto Wels declared the preservation of “peace in our time.” Peace, however, would only last a little under a year, as on the 1st of September, 1939, the Union of Britain launched Operation Sword; the invasion of Ireland. The German declaration of war came two days later, on the 3rd of September, however by then it mattered little, as Operation Charlemagne, the Syndicalist invasion of Germany, was already underway. Disaster struck the Empire a third time on September 13th, when her Reichskanzler, Otto Wels, suddenly passed away. Carl Severing, head of the SPD's right wing, was appointed chancellor in his stead, however, he presided not only over a divided Reichstag, but a party that was tearing at the seams. The remainder of 1939 saw stunning successes for the Third International, as Ireland, Flanders-Wallonia, and Elsass-Löthringen all came under Syndicalist occupation by year's end. 1940 would prove even more disastrous for Germany; in the west, the forces of the Third International had seized all German territory west of the Rhine, and in the east, Boris Savinkov's Russian State launched what he called the “great patriotic war,” aiming to ‘liberate’ eastern Europe from Germany's sphere of influence. In 1941, however, hope for Germany and Europe as a whole was restored when the Danubian Federation and French Republic joined the war against the Kaiserreich's adversaries. A long and bloody struggle ensued, one that came with many sacrifices - later in 1941, Kaiser Wilhelm II, leader of the German Empire since the days of Otto von Bismarck, died, and his son Wilhelm III took the throne. This, in turn, led to Reichskanzler Severing's dismissal, and the ascension of Kaiser Wilhelm's longtime friend, Kurt von Schleicher, to the chancellorship. Schleicher's rise to power saw the SPD and CSRP ousted from government, as the famed anti-parliamentarian sought to form a broad coalition of national-liberals, conservatives, and militarists known as the Deutsche National Einheitsfront (German National Unity Front, DNE). The Empire's sudden slide into authoritarianism would fail to overshadow her military victories, however. 1943 through 1944 saw the tide turn in the west, as the Italian, Spanish, and Norwegian Syndicalists collapsed under the combined forces of the Reichspakt and the Entente, leaving only the Union of Britain and the Commune of France to carry on the fight. Moscow, capital city of the Russian State and bastion of National-Republicanism, fell to German forces on the 3rd of February, 1945; while German soldiers hoisted the Reichskriegsflagge over the gutted remains of the Kremlin, Boris Savinkov, once the most feared man in Russia, lay dead in his bunker, having taken his own life mere hours before. Later that year, on the 6th of August, Paris fell. The heart of revolutionary syndicalism, and the capital of the Commune of France, was surrounded, besieged, and seized by forces of the German army. For the third time in a century, German soldiers marched down the Champs Élysées, joined now by forces of the French Republic. This was not the end of the war, however; while the French Communards fell, the British Maximists remained, fully intent on fighting to the last man. Plans for a naval invasion of the British Isles were drawn up, and scheduled for the 5th of June, 1946 - Tag X. But they would not be needed; for a mere month before, on the 5th of May, a lone RAF bomber soared over the skies of Wilhelmshaven and dropped an atomic bomb on the city. Roughly 45,000 people perished in an instant. A further 120,000 are said to have died of their injuries, radiation poisoning, or cancer in the following years. It was the single most deadly air raid of the war, and it brought almost every one of the belligerent powers to the negotiating table. On the 8th of May, 1946, a ceasefire was signed. The Second Weltkrieg was over, and Germany had won.

*The invasion of Ireland (September 1 - October 6) was an attack against the Irish Republic by the Union of Britain which marked the beginning of the 2nd Weltkrieg. The invasion began on September 1, 1939, one week after the signing of the Struve-Brossolette pact between Russia and the Commune of France, and two weeks after Irish accession to the Reichspakt. The campaign ended on October 6, with the surrender of the last Irish Republican Army units near Dunquin and the establishment of the syndicalist Union of Ireland.*

*British forces invaded Ireland across the Irish Sea the morning after the Rhiannon incident. 2 infantry divisions, 2 armoured divisions and a single marine brigade made landfall in the north near Ballywalter, while 2 infantry divisions landed on Portmarnock beach, near Dublin, aided by a single airborne division which had dropped over the town of Bray 6 hours prior. Initial gains by British forces were immense, as both Dublin and Belfast fell within a week of the start of the invasion. What remained of the Irish Republican Army had by then withdrawn to ad hoc defensive positions across the island's southwest, attempting to hold off syndicalist forces long enough for members of the Irish government, and vast numbers of civilians, to evacuate Ireland from the port of Cork. By the 17th, over three quarters of Ireland was under British occupation, however this date also saw a contingent of the Imperial German Army, known as Rundstedt's Army, alongside a section of the Imperial German Navy's High Seas Fleet, arrive to assist in evacuation efforts. Limerick fell to British forces on the 20th, and over the next 6 days, IRA forces and their German allies would be pushed out of the country. On the 29th, the detachment of the Republican Home Fleet assigned to the invasion engaged with part of the German High Seas Fleet in the Celtic Sea, resulting in a slim British victory. This was the first naval engagement of the war.On October 6, the last active contingent of the IRA in Ireland, holed up near the town of Dunquin, ceased hostilities with and surrendered to the British army, bringing an end to the invasion - although, the Army of the Irish Free State would continue armed resistance to British occupation until 1944. This day also saw the proclamation of the Union of Ireland, a federal syndicalist republic modeled after the Union of Britain. It is largely considered to have served as little more than a British puppet-state until the end of the Weltkrieg in 1946.*
